content: Good evening. So, November is finally fully closed out. I got the final numbers reconciled this afternoon and I've been sitting with them for a few hours now, trying to decide how I feel before I talk through it with anyone. This is the first real full month of operations for Osteria Morishita, and I've been both dreading and looking forward to this review. I want to go through everything line by line because some of it is what I expected, and some of it surprised me in ways I'm still working through. Can we do a full P&L walkthrough?

Good evening, Kenta. Absolutely. A line-by-line walkthrough is exactly the right approach for a first full-month review. It's tempting to anchor on the bottom number and try to make sense of everything from there, but that usually leads to conclusions that aren't fully grounded. If we work through it category by category, you'll understand the structure well enough to make good decisions. I'd suggest we go in order: top-line revenue first, then food cost, then labor, then fixed costs including rent and utilities, then any other costs, then the operating result, and finally cash position and runway. That sequence mirrors how a restaurant P&L actually functions as a system. Does that work, or is there a specific area you want to get to quickly?

Let's go in that order. It's the right way to do it. Okay. Top line. November revenue came in at 3.42 million yen. My target was 4.0 million yen for the month. So I'm short by 580,000 yen against what I had planned. I had built the entire financial model on hitting 4.0M in the first full month, so every cost percentage, every profitability projection, was calibrated to that denominator. When the top line misses by that much, everything downstream shifts. I knew walking into November that we might not hit the target, but I was hoping to get within 10% of it. We came in about 14.5% short.

November revenue of 3.42 million yen against a target of 4.0 million yen. That's a 580,000 yen shortfall, and you've correctly identified why it matters beyond just the absolute number: your fixed costs were sized for a 4.0M denominator, so the percentage structure of your P&L is distorted at this revenue level. A 14.5% miss in the first full month of a new restaurant is something I want to understand before I help you interpret it, because the cause matters a lot. Is the shortfall concentrated in particular service periods, or is it spread across lunch and dinner and all days of the week?

Mostly concentrated, and I have a clear picture of where. Dinner is carrying us — I'd estimate roughly 70% of November revenue came from dinner, 30% from lunch, maybe slightly less. And within dinner, Friday and Saturday have been genuinely strong. We've had some really good rooms on those nights. The energy is right, guests are staying for multiple courses, the check averages are solid. Thursday dinner has been decent too. The real drag is weekday lunch, and Monday lunch specifically has been terrible. I mean that without exaggeration. On the worst Mondays this month, we did five covers at lunch. Five. I'm running a full kitchen crew for five covers. Higashi-Azabu at lunchtime on a Monday just doesn't have the foot traffic to support us. It's a residential neighborhood, it's diplomatic corridors, there are no office towers feeding workers into the street. I knew this intellectually, but I underestimated how badly it would affect the numbers. The other thing is that weeks one and two of November were weaker overall across all service periods. We found better footing in weeks three and four. Word of mouth is starting to build, but it's a slow process.

That's a very clear revenue picture. The geographic reality of Higashi-Azabu is genuinely working against you for weekday lunch. The neighborhood around 3-14-7 Higashi-Azabu draws residents, diplomatic staff, and people with appointments at nearby offices — it is not a walk-in lunch corridor the way Toranomon or the areas closer to Kamiyacho can be. Monday compounds everything: even the neighborhood regulars who might come in for a Wednesday or Thursday lunch tend to be travelling or working from home at the start of the week, and the diplomatic households that make up a meaningful share of your potential clientele are often hosting or attending functions that keep them away from local restaurants on Mondays. The Friday and Saturday dinner strength is the signal I'd focus on most carefully, because it tells you the food, the room, and the service are landing correctly when there are guests in the seats. Guests choosing to stay for multiple courses and generating strong check averages is the validation you need that the core product is working. The revenue problem is a distribution problem — you're getting the right response when people show up, but the seat-fill rate on Monday lunch and in the early weeks of November pulled the total down significantly. One more question before costs: what was the average check across November? And did it vary meaningfully between lunch and dinner, or between the weekday and weekend dinner services?

The check average is actually something I feel reasonably good about. Dinner was averaging around 14,500 to 15,000 yen per head in November. That is roughly where I wanted to be for a tasting-focused Italian concept at this address. Lunch was lower, around 4,000 to 4,500 yen per head, which is expected for a business lunch prix fixe format. The variance between weekday dinner and Friday-Saturday dinner was smaller than I anticipated — Thursday was tracking quite close to Friday in terms of check average. The difference between those evenings was really in covers rather than spend per guest. So when Friday and Saturday nights are strong, it is not just because I am pricing high; it is because the guests are choosing to order more courses and more wine. That is a good sign for the product. Alright, costs. I have the cost breakdown right here and I want to move through it carefully.

Those check averages are solid, and the pattern you described is encouraging. Fourteen to fifteen thousand yen per head at dinner tells you the menu and pricing are in the right range for Higashi-Azabu. The fact that Thursday is tracking close to Friday in average spend rather than covers means your regular weeknight guests are engaged with the full experience, not just coming in for a quick meal. And the Friday-Saturday strength being driven by covers rather than inflated check averages is actually a healthier signal than if it were the other way around — it means you have room to grow revenue on those nights by filling more seats rather than by trying to extract more from the guests already at the table. Okay, let us go through the costs.

Alright. So I have the cost breakdown right in front of me. I'm going to read these to you because I want to make sure we're both looking at exactly the same numbers. The breakdown is: food 31%, labor 38%, rent+utilities 18%, other 9%. That's the full cost structure for November. The sum is 96%, which would theoretically imply a 4% operating margin, but I'll get to why the actual result was different in a moment. Let me just say something about each category before we go further. Food cost at 31% is the one I actually feel okay about. I was targeting 30 to 32%, so 31% is within the range I wanted. My purchasing has been disciplined, the menu pricing is holding up, and I haven't had significant waste issues. That percentage is not where the problem lives. Labor at 38% is the problem. I was modeling 33% in a normal month, and I had a contingency of 35% for a softer month. At 38% I'm well past both thresholds. Rent plus utilities at 18% is fixed — I have a 10-year lease and the rate doesn't move, so that number will look exactly like this every month regardless of revenue. The other 9% covers supplies, credit card processing fees, insurance, professional services, and a few miscellaneous items.

Thank you for reading those out exactly. To confirm what I'm working with: food 31%, labor 38%, rent+utilities 18%, other 9%. That's the cost breakdown for November. Let me reflect back the structural story it tells, because I think it's important to name it clearly before we move to the operating result. Your food cost percentage is in its target range, which means your fundamental unit economics — what you spend on ingredients relative to what you charge — are functioning correctly. Your rent plus utilities at 18% is a fixed obligation that can't be managed down; it's simply a function of the lease you signed. The other 9% is largely fixed or semi-fixed as well. That means the primary problem in this cost structure is labor at 38%, and here is the important thing about that: the labor percentage is high almost entirely because the revenue denominator is lower than your model assumed. Let's do the arithmetic together. If your labor ran at 38% of 3.42 million yen, your actual labor spend was roughly 1.3 million yen for the month. Now ask: what percentage would that same absolute spend represent at your target revenue of 4.0 million yen? It comes out to about 32.5%. That's inside your 33% target. This means your labor cost in absolute terms may not be unreasonably high for the size of operation you're running. It's the revenue shortfall that made the percentage look alarming. That said, this doesn't mean there's nothing to do on the labor side — there may be, and we should discuss it. But the most direct lever you have is revenue recovery. What was the actual operating result for November?

The operating result is a 312,000 yen loss for the month. That's the number I've been sitting with all afternoon. I want to be clear-eyed about it. On one level I knew that the first month or two might be in the red while we build the customer base and the word of mouth accelerates. I had modeled for a breakeven first month at the 4.0 million target, so I understood there was downside risk. But a 312,000 yen loss is real. That's not a rounding error, that's not a timing issue, that's an actual gap between what I'm spending and what I'm bringing in. And it will happen again in December unless I change something. So the question I keep coming back to is not just what drove the loss in November, but what I need to change structurally so that December and the months after it look different.

A 312,000 yen loss for the month. Let me work with that as the operating baseline. You are right to take it seriously rather than rationalize it. First-month losses in a new restaurant are common and often expected, but the question is always whether the loss is structural or transient. A structural loss means the business model does not work at the revenue level you are likely to achieve. A transient loss means you have a ramp-up problem that will correct itself as the customer base builds and the word of mouth compounds. From everything you have told me tonight, November looks more like a transient loss than a structural one. The food cost is within range, the check averages are solid, the Friday and Saturday dinner performance is genuinely encouraging. The loss is driven primarily by the revenue shortfall, which itself is driven by a Monday lunch problem and a slow start to the month. Both of those have addressable causes. That said, transient losses still consume cash, and the runway question is the most important financial question you can ask right now. Have you calculated your cash runway at this burn rate? And are there any significant upcoming expenditures in the next few months that would change the monthly run rate relative to November?

I've done the runway calculation. At current burn, I have 14 months of cash runway. Fourteen months. I went back and forth on whether to tell you that number because it sounds like a lot until you start thinking about what it means practically. Fourteen months sounds comfortable but it isn't, not really. If I drift for five or six months without making structural changes, and the losses continue at this level, I don't have fourteen months anymore — I have eight or nine months, and at eight or nine months I start running out of options. The restaurants I've seen fail didn't fail because they ran out of cash in month one or two. They failed because the operators saw the cash runway and thought they had time, and then they looked up one day and the runway was gone. I don't want to be that person. On upcoming expenditures — nothing major. No equipment purchases planned, no lease changes, no renovations. December's fixed cost base should look very similar to November's. I expect the burn rate to be roughly in the same range unless I change the operating model.

14 months of cash runway at current burn is the parameter we're working within. And the framing you just gave is exactly right. Fourteen months is a defined window, not an open-ended cushion. The danger isn't that you're in crisis today — you're not. The danger is that a fourteen-month runway can become a six-month runway faster than most operators expect if the structural changes don't happen in the near term. The compound math is not in your favor if you wait. At a 312,000 yen monthly loss, you're not at emergency territory, but you are past the point where you can afford to be passive. I want to note something about the November result before we move to decisions. You had a 580,000 yen revenue shortfall, a labor cost percentage that's 3 to 5 percentage points higher than your model, and the result was a 312,000 yen loss. If you close even half of the revenue gap — say you get to 3.7 million yen in December rather than 3.42 million — the math changes considerably, because most of your cost base is fixed. An extra 280,000 yen in revenue on the same fixed cost structure drops mostly to the operating line. That's the leverage you have. Revenue recovery is the primary path to profitability. What decisions have you been thinking about to address the structure of how you're operating?

I've been thinking about it since I closed the books and I've landed on a specific decision. I want to talk it through with you to pressure-test it before I commit. Here is what I'm planning to do. Two pieces, both on the operating hours side. First: I'm going to cut Monday lunch. Full stop. I went through the numbers this afternoon. Eliminating Monday lunch saves me roughly 80,000 yen per month in labor — that's the kitchen and floor staff hours I'm paying for on a service period that generated almost no covers. Against that, I lose maybe 30,000 to 40,000 yen in gross margin from the covers I would have served on those Mondays. So the net improvement is somewhere in the 40,000 to 50,000 yen range per month. Over twelve months, that's 480,000 to 600,000 yen. It also reduces my team's workload on the toughest day of the week, which has some real value for morale and retention that I'm not even trying to quantify. Second piece: on the revenue side, I want to add a late seating on Friday and Saturday evenings. My current model has one seating that starts at 7:00 PM and we turn the room by 9:30. What I want to do is open a second seating at 9:30 PM on Fridays and Saturdays — a tighter menu, maybe four courses instead of the full experience, priced appropriately for a shorter experience. The Higashi-Azabu clientele skews toward later dining — diplomatic community, international residents, finance households. A 9:30 PM seating is not unusual for that demographic. Even filling two or three tables per late seating represents meaningful incremental revenue on the evenings that are already my strongest. So that is the decision: cut Monday lunch, add late seating Friday/Saturday. I believe those two changes together address both sides of the problem — lower costs and higher revenue — and I think they're the right moves. But I want your honest reaction before I pull the trigger.

This is a well-constructed decision, and I think the reasoning is sound. Let me work through each piece carefully, because I want to confirm that the logic holds and surface anything you might not have fully considered before you commit. On cutting Monday lunch: the math you've done is correct. 80,000 yen in labor savings against 30,000 to 40,000 yen in lost gross margin yields a net improvement of 40,000 to 50,000 yen per month. The annualized impact is 480,000 to 600,000 yen, which against a 312,000 yen monthly loss is genuinely meaningful — it could reduce your monthly loss by 13 to 16 percent on its own, without doing anything on the revenue side. There are two things I'd flag for you to think through. First: the communication moment. If you have any regular Monday lunch guests — even a small number — they need to be notified thoughtfully and in advance. In a neighborhood restaurant, losing a regular customer because you closed a service period without notice is a cost that doesn't show up on the P&L but absolutely shows up in future revenue. A two-to-three week notice period, and personal messages to anyone with existing Monday lunch reservations, would protect those relationships. Second: the staff scheduling implications. When you eliminate Monday lunch, you have a choice about whether to reduce total staff hours or redistribute those hours to other service periods. If you're considering redistributing, think about where the hours are most needed — probably Friday and Saturday evening support, which leads directly into your second decision. On adding late seating Friday/Saturday: the demand thesis is compelling for exactly the demographic reasons you named. The international and diplomatic community concentrated in that part of Minato Ward genuinely does tend to eat later, and a 9:30 PM reservation time that would be unusual in Koenji or Sangenjaya is quite normal for the guests you're likely attracting at 3-14-7 Higashi-Azabu. I'd point to three risks to think through carefully. First is staff fatigue. Friday and Saturday are already your highest-volume evenings. Adding a late seating means your kitchen team is working until midnight or later on both nights, after a full first service. That's demanding, and you'll need to be thoughtful about both how you schedule it and how you communicate the change to your staff. The restaurants that add late seatings without managing the human side of that change sometimes find that the incremental revenue doesn't offset the turnover cost. Second is menu discipline. You've already said you want a tighter, more focused menu for the late seating, and that is exactly the right instinct. Four courses rather than the full experience means your kitchen can execute cleanly at 9:30 PM without the full mise en place of the main service. I'd keep the late seating menu extremely tight for the first month — dishes that are simpler to execute, share components with the main menu, and don't require much additional prep. Third is launch strategy. I'd suggest soft-launching the late seating with reservations only for the first four to six weeks. That protects you from the worst-case scenario of staffing a full late service for one table. You can always move to walk-in availability once you've validated the demand. The core decision — cut Monday lunch, add late seating Friday/Saturday — is the right structural move. It addresses the cost side and the revenue side simultaneously, which is the most efficient kind of change when you're working with a 312,000 yen monthly loss and 14 months of cash runway. One final recommendation: set yourself a review trigger point. If you're still running losses above 200,000 yen per month by the end of February or early March, revisit the full schedule and staffing model at that point rather than waiting until the runway has dropped below six months. You want to course-correct while you still have time and meaningful options available.

The staff fatigue point is the one I was least focused on, and you're right to raise it. My kitchen team has been running hard. I hadn't fully thought through what adding a 9:30 PM seating on both Friday and Saturday does to them cumulatively over a month. I need to have a real conversation with my chef before I announce anything externally. The reservations-only launch is also the right call — I don't know why I wasn't already planning that, but I wasn't. I was thinking of it as an open second seating, which is clearly wrong. Alright. I think I have a clear picture. November revenue shortfall was real, the cost structure is manageable if I can close the revenue gap, the 312,000 yen monthly loss is the number I have to work against, and I have 14 months to fix it — but only if I start moving now. The two-part schedule change is the first structural move. I'll talk to my chef tomorrow and get staff input before I finalize the timeline for implementing the late seating. Thank you for working through this with me.

That is the right sequence. The chef conversation has to come before the external announcement, both because your chef's input may genuinely affect how you structure the late seating menu and timing, and because asking for input rather than announcing a decision is how you protect the relationship that matters most to running those Friday and Saturday nights well. A chef who feels consulted will approach the late seating as a creative opportunity. A chef who feels informed after the fact will approach it as an added burden. The distinction matters a great deal for how the late seating actually performs in the first few weeks. Let me summarize what you have decided and what comes next, so you have a clean record. November result: revenue of 3.42 million yen against a 4.0M target, cost breakdown of food 31%, labor 38%, rent+utilities 18%, other 9%, operating loss of 312,000 yen for the month. Cash runway at current burn is 14 months. Structural decisions confirmed: cut Monday lunch to recover approximately 40,000 to 50,000 yen per month net, and add late seating Friday/Saturday to build incremental revenue on your strongest service periods. Immediate next steps: chef conversation tomorrow on feasibility, menu structure, and scheduling implications; communication plan for regular Monday lunch guests with at least two to three weeks of notice; reservations-only soft launch for the late seating to validate demand before committing to full staffing on those nights. Set a review trigger: if losses are still running above 200,000 yen per month by end of February, revisit the full schedule and staffing model at that point rather than waiting until the runway has dropped below six months. You are making decisions with the right information and moving at the right pace. Come back once you have talked to your chef and we will work through the implementation details together.
